questions.explanation: In formal offers, 'shall I' is the standard polite form with first person.
questions.q: ___ open the window for you?

questions.explanation: In legal and regulatory texts, 'shall' imposes an obligation, equivalent to 'must'.
questions.q: All members ___ submit their returns by 31 March.

questions.explanation: The rhetorical 'shall' with 'we' proposes joint action in formal style.
questions.q: Choose the most formal way to suggest moving on with the agenda.

questions.explanation: Formal suggestions of joint action use 'shall we'; 'will we' sounds like a question about the future.
questions.q: Complete the tag-style invitation correctly.

questions.explanation: In contracts, 'shall' creates a binding duty; 'may' would only grant permission.
questions.q: The contractor ___ disclose confidential information to third parties.

questions.explanation: 'Shall' in the main clause after 'if' states a formal consequence or rule.
questions.q: If the regulations are breached, ___.

questions.explanation: A formal offer to a guest uses 'shall I', not the casual 'do you want me to'.
options: Do you want me to take your coat?
questions.q: Choose the most formal offer to a dinner guest.

questions.explanation: 'Shall' with first-person questions asks for instruction or permission in formal registers.
questions.q: ___ read the first clause aloud?

questions.explanation: Formal minutes record a resolution with 'shall', giving it binding force.
questions.q: The committee resolved that the treasurer ___ prepare the accounts.

questions.explanation: Only 'shall' gives the rule its formal, authoritative tone; the others soften or misstate it.
options: Visitors may not smoke in the hall.
Visitors should not smoke in the hall.
Visitors must not smoke in the hall.
Visitors shall not smoke in the hall.
questions.q: Choose the version that reads as an official regulation.

questions.explanation: A formal toast uses 'shall we' to propose the action jointly and politely.
options: Let's raise our glasses, will we
questions.q: Complete the formal toast: 'Ladies and gentlemen, ___.'

questions.explanation: 'Shall' is the traditional future with first person in formal British style, not a subjunctive.
questions.q: We ___ overcome these difficulties together. (formal, traditional)

questions.explanation: In an interrogative offer, 'shall' pairs with first person; 'will' would ask about willingness awkwardly.
questions.q: ___ begin the examination?

questions.explanation: 'Shall' states the regulation authoritatively; 'can' merely describes ability.
questions.q: Each applicant ___ provide two references.

questions.explanation: The negative formal prohibition in rules uses 'shall not', not the casual 'mustn't'.
questions.q: Mobile phones ___ used during the ceremony.

questions.explanation: A formal direction to a colleague uses 'shall we' for joint action, not the imperative.
questions.q: ___ adjourn for lunch and reconvene at two?

questions.explanation: 'Shall I' offers assistance formally; 'Will I' would be unidiomatic here.
questions.q: ___ fetch you another chair?

questions.explanation: In solemn declarations, 'shall' marks a binding commitment, stronger than 'will'.
questions.q: The witness ___ tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

questions.explanation: 'Shall' in a formal question seeks guidance; 'do I have to' sounds reluctant.
questions.q: Choose the formal way to ask the chair for direction.

questions.explanation: Formal notices use 'shall' to impose the requirement; 'are to' is weaker.
questions.q: All delegates ___ wear their badges at all times.
